name: Neck Crank Recognition
description: Learn to distinguish between a safe choke (strangle) and a dangerous neck crank. A crank attacks the cervical spine via pressure on the chin or back of the head rather than the carotid arteries, and must be recognized immediately to tap or adjust.
shortInstruction: If you feel pressure on the chin or back of the head (not the sides of the neck), you are being cranked, not choked. Tap early and protect your cervical spine.
summary: Neck crank recognition is the ability to instantly distinguish between a blood choke (strangle) that targets the carotid arteries and a neck crank that targets the cervical spine. A blood choke is safe to train with a training partner — it cuts off blood flow to the brain and causes unconsciousness without structural damage. A neck crank attacks the vertebrae, discs, and ligaments of the cervical spine and can cause cumulative damage over training years. The key difference: chokes apply pressure to the sides of the neck (carotid), cranks apply pressure to the chin, back of the head, or top of the spine.
whyItWorks: Blood chokes are safe because they interrupt blood flow without damaging neck structures — unconsciousness is reversible with no lasting effects
Neck cranks are dangerous because they compress, rotate, or hyperflex the cervical spine — the damage is cumulative and can lead to chronic issues
The chin is the most reliable indicator — if the pressure is on your chin pushing your head toward your chest or shoulder, it is a crank
Carotid pressure (sides of the neck) with no chin/spine pressure is always a choke and is safe to defend
commonMistakes: Assuming every hand-on-neck attack is a choke — many are disguised cranks
Trying to 'tough out' a neck crank thinking it will 'come on' like a choke — cranks do not resolve, they only get worse
Not tapping early enough to neck cranks in training — the damage accumulates over months and years
Confusing a can opener (crank) with a collar choke (safe) — both can be applied from guard but have completely different mechanisms
coachingCues: Side neck pressure = choke, defend safely
If unsure, tap — protect the neck
safetySummary: Neck cranks can cause disc herniation, ligament sprains, nerve impingement, and chronic neck pain
The can opener (pushing the back of the head toward the chest from guard) is the most common dangerous crank in BJJ
The twister (spinal lock from back control) aggressively rotates the cervical spine and can cause serious injury if applied suddenly
Some guillotine and D'Arce variations can become neck cranks if the angle is off — if you feel chin pressure, tap and re-set
Even mild neck cranks cause cumulative damage — do not accept 10 'light' cranks per week as normal training
keyCorrections: If you feel chin pressure during a submission attempt: tap immediately — do not wait to see if it 'turns into' a choke
If your training partner consistently applies neck cranks instead of chokes: have a conversation with them about technique and safety
If you are the attacker and your partner taps to a position you thought was a choke: re-examine your angle — you may be cranking without realizing it

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Neck crank recognition requires understanding the three types of neck attacks: blood choke, air choke, and neck crank

decisionTree.action: Blood choke (strangle): pressure is applied to the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck. Cause unconsciousness by preventing oxygenated blood from reaching the brain. Structure: cross-collar, rear-naked, triangle, guillotine (when correctly applied), baseball bat. Safe to train with controlled application

Air choke: pressure is applied to the trachea/windpipe. Causes difficulty breathing but does not cut off blood flow. Structure: front choke, some cross-collar variations, some baseball bat variations. Higher injury risk than blood choke

decisionTree.condition: Neck crank: pressure is applied to the cervical spine via the chin, back of the head, or base of the skull. Structure: can opener, twister, some guillotine variations (when rolled), some D'Arce variations, some triangle variations. NOT safe to train aggressively

decisionTree.action: Recognition rule: if you feel pressure on the sides of your neck (near the jaw bone) = likely a blood choke. If you feel pressure on your chin, back of head, or top of spine = definitely a crank
Response rule: blood choke = defend or escape. Neck crank = tap immediately if significant pressure is applied

moneyDetails: Neck crank recognition prevents the most common source of chronic training injuries in BJJ — cumulative neck damage
Knowing the difference between a crank and a choke allows you to train submissions safely at full intensity
Protecting your neck for 10+ years of training requires disciplined tapping to cranks in every training session
A healthy neck at age 50 is worth more than any tap you avoided at age 25
fixItFast: If you feel chin or spine pressure: tap immediately — you lose absolutely nothing by tapping early to a neck crank
If you feel ambiguous pressure (unsure if crank or choke): tap — uncertainty means it is probably not a clean choke
If your neck feels stiff or sore after training: you are not tapping early enough to cranks. Prioritize neck protection
